Higher nominal wages are a certainty, of course, but do job losses offset this? Does a higher minimum wage lead to inflation that leaves purchasing power unchanged?
On balance and in aggregate, is a higher minimum wage good for low wage employees or does it hurt them more than it helps?

I've noticed this question come up a few times over the last week or so. I'm not a labor economist, but it's my understanding that the effect of an increase in a minimum wage is far from certain. Some academic papers have found no effect on employment following an increase in the minimum wage, while others have found some effect. It seems that an increase in the minimum wage will lead to some things becoming more expensive, particularly in industries where minimum wage labor plays a central role in the production process (e.g. fast food). Whether this price increase offsets the additional earnings minimum wage workers get is not certain. For example, it might be that people change their consumption bundles and move away from eating fast food (for example), and employment in fast food decreases. OR it might be that since minimum wage workers can now afford MORE (or the same amount of) fast food and there is an increase in demand. The economy is super complex and I'm not sure even the most sophisticated model can truly account for all the changes stemming from an increase in the minimum wage. However, from a social perspective, it seems reasonable that people who work 40+ hours week in any occupation should be able to afford basic items such as food, housing and transportation. In many places in the U.S., this isn't possible with the current minimum wage.

There is a comparative advantage factor involving minimum wage. I think setting it at 1.5% of the average one bedroom apartment within city limits would have several benefits. It would attract start ups to areas in need of economic development. It might cut down on commuter traffic and emissions, since workers could afford to live in the communities they work in. It would also control rent inflation.

On the downside, hours would likely be cut to compensate for the wage increase. Cheap fast food wouldn't be available in upscale areas. And developers will probably build more low cost housing in upscale areas, lowering the property value. Property value would go up in low income areas as commuter take home pay increases. More young people and immigrants would work under the table for less than min wage. But I can live with all that.
